Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed
issues.explanation: For an 18-year-old whose index trauma is witnessing domestic violence in childhood, this appraisal is hard to reconcile with the likely role in the trauma. A child witness may feel guilty, but 'I should have protected others' implies a level of responsibility and agency that is clinically implausible enough to question for this trauma context. The rest of the profile coheres around fear, helplessness, fragmented sensory memory, and hypervigilant threat monitoring; this single appraisal stands out as inconsistent with the demographics/trauma role.

vignette: James was only a child when he witnessed his father's violent outbursts against his mother. The memories of those terrifying moments were etched into his mind with vivid detail. He remembered the sound of breaking glass and the way his mother's voice would tremble as she tried to calm his father down. One particular night stood out: his father had thrown a vase across the room, and it shattered against the wall just inches from where James was hiding under the kitchen table. The silence that followed was even more chilling, making him feel like something worse was about to happen. As he grew older, these memories didn't fade; instead, they became more potent triggers for his discomfort. Unexpected touches, especially in crowded places, would send a jolt of panic through him. He often felt uncomfortable around people who seemed suspicious or unpredictable, as if they might suddenly turn violent. This discomfort was not just an isolated feeling but one that frequently brought back the snapshots of those traumatic moments. Each time he remembered, his body would tense up, mimicking the positions he had taken to protect himself during the abuse. James's fear of going crazy began to take hold when he noticed how his reactions were becoming more intense and unpredictable. He often found himself avoiding unfamiliar places, where he couldn't assess the danger or control the environment. In these settings, unusual silence made him feel on edge, as if it signaled an impending threat. His hyper-vigilance extended to noticing potential weapons or dangerous objects in any room, a habit that had become ingrained over time. These negative appraisals of himself and his situation deepened his sense of helplessness. He felt like he couldn't stop bad things from happening to him, just as he had been unable to protect his mother during those violent episodes. This helplessness fueled his fear of going crazy, making him doubt his own sanity and reliability. Every time a memory surfaced, it reinforced these negative beliefs. The overwhelming grief that accompanied the memories made him feel like he was losing control, further solidifying his belief that he couldn't rely on himself. The cycle of triggers, threats, and negative appraisals became self-reinforcing. When James felt threatened by silence or potential weapons, it triggered more memories of the abuse, which in turn heightened his sense of threat. These moments were not just fleeting; they built into a persistent pattern that began to affect his daily life. As a police officer, he found himself constantly on edge, always scanning for signs of danger. This hyper-vigilance made it difficult for him to trust his colleagues or relax during off-duty hours. The memories and the threats they brought with them also led James to avoid social interactions. He became isolated, preferring to stay in familiar environments where he felt a sense of control. However, this isolation only reinforced his negative appraisals, making him feel more helpless and out of touch with reality. The grief that came with each memory further compounded his fear of losing his mind. Despite his efforts to manage these symptoms, the strain became too much. James's performance at work began to suffer, and he received a warning from his supervisor about his increasingly erratic behavior. What frightened him most was the realization that he might not be able to protect others if he couldn't even protect himself. This fear, along with the overwhelming grief and helplessness, finally brought him to seek help. When James first walked into the therapist's office, he was filled with a mix of hope and dread. He hoped that therapy could provide some relief from the constant cycle of triggers, threats, and negative appraisals. But he was also afraid that it might confirm his worst fears-that he was indeed going crazy and that there was no way to escape the memories that haunted him. Despite these fears, James was determined to find a way forward, to break the cycle and regain control over his life.
